'''Debra Toby Silverman''' (born December 31, 1948) is an American biostatistician and epidemiologist specialized in [[bladder cancer]] epidemiology and the [[carcinogenicity]] of [[diesel exhaust]]. Silverman is the chief of the occupational and environmental epidemiology branch at the [[National Cancer Institute]]. 

== Life ==
Silverman was born December 31, 1948.<ref name=":2" /> She completed a B.A. in Mathematics at [[Brooklyn College]] in June 1970.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Silverman, Debra 2022 - Office of NIH History and Stetten Museum |url=https://history.nih.gov/display/history/Silverman,+Debra+2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908132533/https://history.nih.gov/display/history/Silverman%2C+Debra+2022 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 8, 2022 |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=history.nih.gov}}{{PD-notice}}</ref> Silverman earned a Sc.M. in [[health statistics]] from the [[Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=1980-01-01 |title=Debra T. Silverman, Sc.D., biographical sketch and research interests - NCI |url=https://dceg.cancer.gov/about/staff-directory/silverman-debra |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=dceg.cancer.gov |language=en}}{{PD-notice}}</ref> Her master's degree was funded by a [[U.S. Public Health Service]] traineeship. Her 1972 thesis was titled ''Maternal smoking and birth weight''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite thesis |last=Silverman |first=Debra Toby |title=Maternal smoking and birth weight |date=1972 |degree=Sc.M. |publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University]] |oclc=8938252}}</ref> Her advisor was [[James Tonascia]].<ref name=":2" /> Professor [[George W. Comstock]] had suggested the idea for her thesis and allowed Silverman to use data collected during the 1963 [[Washington County, Maryland]] census.<ref name=":2" /> When Silverman completed her training in [[Baltimore]], she interviewed for a number of positions at the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) and was not sure which institute to join.<ref name=":1" /> Silverman asked [[Abraham Lilienfeld]], who was chair of epidemiology at Johns Hopkins University, what he thought. And he said, "Oh, go to cancer. That’s where all the money was."<ref name=":1" /> This was in 1972; the [[National Cancer Act]] was passed in 1971 and the field was growing tremendously.<ref name=":1" /> Silverman joined the [[National Cancer Institute]] (NCI) as a [[biostatistician]] in 1972.<ref name=":0" /> 

After three years at NCI, Silverman decided to go back to school to get her doctorate. NCI paid her tuition and full salary.<ref name=":1" /> In 1981, she completed a Sc.D. in epidemiology from the [[Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health]].<ref name=":0" /> Her doctoral studies built on previous bladder cancer epidemiologic research conducted by her professor [[Philip Cole (epidemiologist)|Philip Cole]] and her mentor [[Robert N. Hoover]].<ref name=":1" /> Her dissertation was titled, ''A case-control study of lower-urinary-tract cancer in Detroit''.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Silverman |first=Debra Toby |title=A case-control study of lower-urinary-tract cancer in Detroit |date=1981 |degree=Sc.D. |publisher=[[Harvard School of Public Health]]}}</ref> Silverman returned to NCI and has worked as a [[Cancer epidemiology|cancer epidemiologist]] since 1983.<ref name=":0" /> During the mid-1980s into the 1990s, her supervisor, [[Joseph F. Fraumeni Jr.]] allowed Silverman, and her colleagues [[Shelia Hoar Zahm]] and [[Patricia Hartge]] to all work part-time so they could raise families.<ref name=":1" /> She was part-time for 16 years, having her first daughter in 1986.<ref name=":1" /> [[Alan S. Morrison]] served as an additional mentor of Silverman.<ref name=":1" />  

Silverman is chief of the NCI Occupational and Environmental Epidemiology Branch (OEEB) within the Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics (DCEG).<ref name=":0" /> In November 2024, Silverman will retire from the NCI after 16 years as Director of the OEEB. <ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-17 |title=Debra Silverman to Retire from the NCI - NCI |url=https://dceg.cancer.gov/news-events/news/2024/silverman-retirement |access-date=2025-09-21 |website=dceg.cancer.gov |language=en}}</ref> 

She specializes in [[bladder cancer]] epidemiology and the [[carcinogenicity]] of [[diesel exhaust]].<ref name=":1" />  

==Awards==
Silverman has received awards, including the Harvard School of Public Health Alumni Award of Merit for the scientific importance and public health impact of her research; the PHS Special Recognition Award for research on environmental determinants of bladder and other cancers; the [[American Occupational Medical Association]] Merit in Authorship Award for her contributions to a paper on a job/exposure linkage system; the NIH Director’s Award, the NCI Special Act Award, the [[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health|NIOSH]] Alice Hamilton Science Award for Occupational Safety and Health, and the [[British Occupational Hygiene Society]] Award in recognition of her work on the Diesel Exhaust in Miners Study; the NIH Merit Award for her contributions to pancreatic cancer research; and the DCEG Exemplary Service and Investigator Award.<ref name=":0" /> Silverman is an elected member of the [[American Epidemiological Society]] and a Fellow of the [[American College of Epidemiology]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Principal Investigators |url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/debra-silverman |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=NIH Intramural Research Program |language=en}}</ref>
